tier_reason: benchmarks/wasi/RESULTS.md compares the Silverfir JIT with wasmtime Cranelift 47.0.2 (built from source, rustc 1.97.0) and V8 (Node 25.9.0, V8 14.1.146) on an Apple M4; the harness (benchmarks/wasi/run_tests.py, run_v8.mjs) and the guest build (benchmarks/wasi/Makefile: wasi-sdk clang -O2 --target=wasm32-wasip1, committed .wasm shared by every engine) are public, and Silverfir's release profile (lto, codegen-units=1, opt-level=3) is in Cargo.toml. Gaps that keep it borderline A: the wasi-sdk version and the wasm3 build (commit, flags) are not stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Guests: wasi-sdk clang (version not stated) -O2 --target=wasm32-wasip1 via benchmarks/wasi/Makefile, binaries committed and shared by all engines. Silverfir: cargo --release, workspace profile lto=true, codegen-units=1, opt-level=3. wasmtime Cranelift and Winch 47.0.2 built from source with rustc 1.97.0; Node 25.9.0 (V8 14.1.146); wasm3 '~/Dev/wasm3 build-release' (commit and flags not stated); wasmi_cli 2.0.0-beta.7 via cargo install (CoreMark cell 2.0.0-beta.10). Harness: benchmarks/wasi/run_tests.py and run_v8.mjs.
corrections.caveats: First-party suite, one machine (M4), interpreters are single runs (author says treat as +/-5%) while compiled engines are the mean of two rounds; Cranelift still wins 9 of 15 metrics and is ahead on sqlite and LZ4 decompress (3,478 vs 3,241), so the JIT claim is parity, not a win. Wasmtime 47.0.2 and V8 14.1 are older than current releases (wasmtime v49 was current in September 2026); the numbers are dated 2026-07-24/25 and share no baseline with earlier revisions of the file. CoreMark runs in a non-standard bounded regression mode, except the interpreter CoreMark row, which was refreshed on 2026-08-31 with standalone scores and uses wasmi 2.0.0-beta.10 rather than beta.7. The wasm3 build compared against is not pinned to a version. The sqlite and Lua rows are historical (the active suite has changed those benchmarks). Independent cross-check in the wasmi-benchmarks suite (wasmi-labs, AMD EPYC 7763, plot raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg, date not stated, 23 runtime configurations): execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is Silverfir interpreter 9.02 vs Wasmi v2 12.40, Wasm3 16.51, WAMR fast-interp 17.07 and Pulley 27.92 (fastest interpreter, about 1.37x ahead of Wasmi v2, derived from page data), and Silverfir JIT 1.25 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15, Wasmer Cranelift 1.17 and V8 1.05, so the JIT trails the optimizing compilers slightly on that suite. That suite is run by the author of wasmi, a competing interpreter.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches RESULTS.md (SHA-256 250.6 vs 216.8, bzip2 30.68 vs 26.86, CoreMark 44,958/45,874/44,378, mandelbrot 1.68x over V8, interpreter 1.16-2.01x over wasm3, 1.07-2.41x over wasmi, 1.07-1.69x over the faster rival, median about 1.39x). Shortcomings: JIT only at parity with Cranelift (9 of 15 rows to Cranelift), interpreter numbers single runs, baseline wasmtime 47.0.2 one major version old, wasm3 build unpinned, CoreMark in non-standard bounded mode, 67 stars. The wasmi-benchmarks plot independently ranks its interpreter first among the interpreter configurations and its JIT just behind Cranelift and V8.

tier_reason: Independent harness rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (crates/benchmark-core/src/cases.rs, scripts/build-wamr.sh, scripts/run-m4-pass.sh, all public) measures WAMR fast-interp against wasmtime v49 Pulley with Apple clang 21.0.0, stated flags (cmake Release -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, AOT/JIT off; Pulley --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO) on M4 Max E-cores and an A12; results are consensus-checked so wrong answers fail the row.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime over the 17 cases all seven runtimes run (lower is better): M4 Max E-cores WAMR fast-interp 1.63 vs Wasmtime Pulley 2.09 and WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; iPhone XS (A12) E-cores 1.38 vs 1.68 and 9.28. About 1.28x faster than Pulley on the M4 and 1.22x on the A12 (derived from page data). Per case on M4 (CPU ms per call): bulk_memory 10.41 vs 22.14, call_indirect 18.48 vs 31.53, convolution 3.928 vs 5.883, sieve 0.5128 vs 0.7082. The harness repo's earlier docs/cross-runtime-pulley-vs-wamr.md (iPhone 12, 2026-05-15, Pulley with the author's phase-3 fusion patches) has WAMR 1.37-1.86x faster on call_indirect, xmrsplayer, graphql (AssemblyScript) and the vtable suite.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: WAMR main (WAMR-2.4.1-364, b70d708d, 2026-09-21) with 29 local patches, cmake Release -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 BULK_MEMORY=1 TAIL_CALL=1 etc., WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1; Pulley from wasmtime v49 fork (9 extra commits), rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12, fat LTO, 1 CGU; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0).
corrections.caveats: WAMR is itself a category baseline; listed for its measured wins over Wasmtime's Pulley interpreter and, in AOT mode, over JIT runtimes. The win is interpreter versus interpreter, not versus Wasmtime's native Cranelift JIT. Pulley is not ahead everywhere: it beats WAMR on fib (1.13 vs 1.38 relative on M4), fib_tail, tailcall_fsm and extconst_init. In the same harness WAMR is slower than wasm3 (1.63 vs 1.01 geomean) and level with wasmz (1.59 on M4, 1.63 on A12). The benchmarked WAMR is unreleased main (the latest release, 2.4.5, lacks 364 of those commits) carrying 29 patches by the benchmark author (legacy EH, relaxed SIMD, PROT_NONE linear memory), and the Pulley side is a fork with 9 extra commits (including call_indirect argument bundling). Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. AOT evidence (derived from page data, reproduced by the verifier): in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12 libsodium CSVs (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2022-12/res/iwasm.csv with wasmtime.csv, wasmer-cranelift.csv, wasmer-llvm.csv, node.csv, native.csv) the iwasm geomean time over the 61 tests common to all six files is 0.665x Wasmtime, 0.688x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.794x Wasmer LLVM and 0.588x Node/V8, and 2.30x native; the CSVs do not say iwasm ran in AOT mode (inferred from magnitude; CPU and flags not in the repo, and no README for that run). In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test, date not stated) WAMR fast-interp is 17.07 vs Pulley 27.92, but behind Wasm3 16.51, Wasmz 15.89, Wasmi v2 12.40 and Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02. WAMR wiki (https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/wiki/Performance, i7-7700, GCC 7.5.0 -O3, 2020-09-01) compares only against wasm3 and native.

notes: All numbers check against runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md (geomeans 1.63/2.09 M4 and 1.38/1.68 A12; per-case ms) and docs/cross-runtime-pulley-vs-wamr.md (1.37-1.86x). The current merged record for this id (folded from the wasm and jit searches) also carries the libsodium 2022-12 AOT claim; I recomputed it from the CSVs and got the same 0.665/0.688/0.794/0.588/2.30 geomeans, but the run's mode, CPU and flags are unstated, so that part is tier C at best. Shortcomings: win is only over the Pulley interpreter, Pulley wins 4 cases, slower than wasm3, measured build is patched unreleased main.

tier_reason: Independent public harness (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark: crates/benchmark-core/src/cases.rs, scripts/build-wasm3.sh with COMMON_CFLAGS -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, scripts/run-m4-pass.sh) runs unpatched wasm3 v0.9.0 against WAMR fast-interp and wasmtime v49 Pulley with Apple clang 21.0.0 on M4 Max E-cores and an A12, N=10, results consensus-checked.

corrections.caveats: Result is interpreter versus interpreter: wasm3 is not faster than JIT/AOT Wasmtime, Wasmer or V8 (its own docs/Performance.md CoreMark table, 2019-2020 on an i5-8250U and labelled historical by the project, has wasmtime 0.8.0 and Wasmer Cranelift 4.0x faster and wasm-micro-runtime 8.1x slower; in the wasmi-benchmarks suite on an AMD EPYC 7763 its execute geomean is 16.51 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15 and V8 1.05, and behind Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02 and Wasmi v2 12.40). The 17-case geomean covers only MVP/scalar code: wasm3 cannot run the SIMD-canonical builds, exceptions, GC, typed references, memory64 or multi-memory, and WAMR leads on the SIMD rows. Instantiation is its weak spot: extended-const modules cost it 116-122x Pulley's time on the M4 (62-85x on the A12). The benchmark author built WAMR with 29 carried patches, WasmEdge with 26 and Pulley from a fork branch with 9 extra commits, while wasm3 v0.9.0 ran unpatched. Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test', native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR. The README still declares a minimal maintenance phase, though September 2026 commits add atomics and an exception-handling API.

notes: Numbers match the page: geomeans wasm3 1.01, wasmz 1.59, WAMR 1.63, Pulley 2.09, tinywasm 3.20, WasmEdge 8.42 (M4) and 1.04/1.38/1.68 (A12); call_indirect 11.67 vs 18.48 vs 31.53 ms; the libsodium quote is verbatim. Metadata checked: MIT, 8.0k stars, last commit 2026-09-29. Shortcomings: interpreter-only win, far slower than JIT runtimes, no SIMD/GC/EH/memory64 so its geomean covers MVP code only, slow instantiation of extended-const modules.
